newsitem.title: UK: Copper ends LME easier, tightness beats a retreat.
newsitem.headline: Copper ends LME easier, tightness beats a retreat.

text.p: Copper trading remained volatile during Monday afternoon trading on the LME, as an extreme technical squeeze on nearby supplies unravelled viciously.

The cash/threes backwardation, which stood at $210 at one stage, narrowed to $87/97 at the close, as waves of lending knocked the stuffing out of the market, pulling forward prices down in their wake.
"This market is totally confused...but the short-term fundamentals are supportive, which is playing into the hands of the longs," said Angus MacMillan, analyst at LME broker Billiton Metals Ltd.
The squeeze is taking place against a background of supply disputes in Chile, the world's largest producer, falling global stocks, and a temporary closure of the big Kennecott smelter in the U.S.
Traders said that this has coincided with major short positions falling due.
"There is a big short that keeps on getting rolled forward. It happened at the end of October, January, end-April, and is now being pushed to the end of July," one said.
Nearby premiums could now contract further, although many remain wary of further tightness.
"As long as the stocks are low and still falling there is still the potential for further squeezes," MacMillan said.
Copper stocks are forecast to fall further in the short-term, as metal is delivered out of Singapore.
"The tightness is there to May 3, so it is not over yet," another trader said.

Three months prices, meanwhile, were nervy after hitting an early peak of $2,407, and fell rapidly as the spreads collapsed. By the end of the kerb the market was at $2,356, down $27 from Friday's kerb close.
Prices held just above the $2,350 level, but today's technical action and close is poor, which suggests that the downside will be tested again.
Despite the wide price moves and the extent of the backwardation contraction, volumes and liquidity were not large in copper. Business in other metals was also not significant.
"They have mostly been whipped around by copper," MacMillan said.
Aluminium was an exception, building constructively above $1,600 against a background of technical tightness in early July, belived to reflect fund covering.
Although prices were unable to clear $1,640, last trade at $1,628.50 was still $15.50 up from the previous kerb.
Lead and zinc turned tail from steadier levels, and finished at $630 and $1,267, down $1 and $8 respectively.
Nickel closed $20 easier at $7,460, while tin was down $10 at $5,730. Alloy was indicated at $1,505/15. - London Newsroom +00 44 171 542 7729 --Martin Hayes, London Newsroom 44 171 542 8080
